facts.raw_span: A 40-year-old man from eastern India presented with a nonhealing ulcer on the tongue present for the last 4 months
The lesion started as a small painless mass on the right lateral aspect of the tongue, which gradually grew and subsequently ulcerated
No history of trauma or tongue bite preceding the lesion
Patient denied consuming tobacco or alcohol regularly
Medical history includes well-controlled type 2 diabetes mellitus for 2 years with oral hypoglycemic agents
Single well-defined ulcer measuring 2 × 2 cm on the right lateral aspect of tongue with a clean base and irregular and elevated heaped-up margins
No underlying induration, friability, or bleeding on manipulation
Dense diffuse infiltrate of lymphocytes, histiocytes, epithelioid cells, giant cells, plasma cells, eosinophils, and neutrophils
Many histiocytes and giant cells contained intracellular yeasts with a surrounding halo
Special stains (Grocott-Gomori methenamine-silver nitrate and periodic acid–Schiff) highlighted fungal forms
Fungal culture on Sabouraud dextrose agar was negative
HIV-1 and HIV-2 serologic testing were negative

concepts.why: Intracellular yeasts with a surrounding halo were found in histiocytes, suggesting a fungal infection, and the patient's presentation with a nonhealing ulcer on the tongue is consistent with oral histoplasmosis.
The presence of a dense diffuse infiltrate of lymphocytes and histiocytes, along with the finding of fungal forms, suggests a fungal infection such as oral candidiasis.

concepts.preferred_label: Squamous Cell Carcinoma of the Tongue
concepts.why: The patient's presentation with a nonhealing ulcer on the tongue, which started as a small painless mass, is concerning for a malignant process such as squamous cell carcinoma.
The patient's history of well-controlled type 2 diabetes mellitus and the presence of a nonhealing ulcer on the tongue suggest a possible association between the two conditions.

concepts.preferred_label: Chronic Traumatic Ulcer of the Tongue
concepts.why: The patient's denial of trauma or tongue bite preceding the lesion makes this diagnosis less likely, but it cannot be entirely ruled out.
The presence of a dense diffuse infiltrate of lymphocytes and histiocytes, along with the finding of giant cells, suggests a possible tuberculous infection.
The patient's presentation with a nonhealing ulcer on the tongue without a clear cause or association with other conditions suggests a possible idiopathic origin.
The finding of intracellular yeasts with a surrounding halo and the presence of fungal forms suggest a fungal infection of the tongue.
The presence of intracellular yeasts within histiocytes and giant cells, along with negative HIV serologic testing, points towards Histoplasmosis as a possible diagnosis.

rationales.F02: Painless mass on the tongue could be a sign of malignancy
rationales.F03: No history of trauma reduces the likelihood of traumatic ulcer
rationales.F04: No tobacco or alcohol use reduces the risk of oral cancer
rationales.F05: Diabetes is a risk factor for oral infections and ulcers
rationales.F08: Mixed cell infiltrate is a sign of chronic infection or inflammation
rationales.F09: Intracellular yeasts are a hallmark of histoplasmosis
rationales.F10: Fungal forms on special stains confirm fungal infection
rationales.F11: Negative fungal culture does not rule out fungal infection
